PRO FORMA FIRST BOARD RESOLUTION
The sole shareholder of the Company, acting unanimously, resolves as follows:
1. To approve the draft Articles of Association (Estatutos Sociales) of the Company, which include the corporate name, registered office in Spain, share capital of Three Thousand Euros (3,000 EUR), and the corporate purpose of providing maritime seafarer recruitment and crew management services.

4. To authorize the Administrator to perform all acts necessary for incorporation, including opening corporate bank accounts and obtaining the required maritime crewing agency license from the DGMM.
This resolution is adopted on the date of incorporation and is effective immediately.

Stage 03

Tax Identity & Indirect Tax

Tax authority e-portal, entity tax classification elections, VAT thresholds, and 0% export documentation chain.

Tax ID Application Infrastructure

Competent tax authority

Agencia Estatal de Administración Tributaria (AEAT), including its electronic headquarters (Sede Electrónica); regional tax authorities administer certain taxes in the Basque Country and Navarre, but the target jurisdiction is Spain under the common tax regime.

E-government filing portal

A Spanish Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada (SL) obtains its Spanish tax identification number (NIF) from the AEAT, normally by filing Form 036 for census registration. The company may initially receive a provisional NIF and must provide the required incorporation and registration evidence to obtain or confirm its definitive NIF. A foreign legal entity generally applies using Form 036, supporting evidence of legal existence and authority to act, and identification documents for its representative; documents may require apostille or legalization and certified Spanish translation. A non-established taxable person making Spanish VAT-taxable supplies must register before commencing those supplies. A taxable person established outside the EU may be required to appoint a Spanish fiscal representative for VAT purposes, subject to applicable statutory exceptions and mutual-assistance arrangements. A separate EU VAT identification number is obtained through AEAT registration in the relevant census; VIES validation is available for qualifying intra-Community operators.

Tax ID type & application path: Entity_Level_Taxation — A Spanish Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada (SL) obtains its Spanish tax identification number (NIF) from the AEAT, normally by filing Form 036 for census registration. The company may initially receive a provisional NIF and must provide the required incorporation and registration evidence to obtain or confirm its definitive NIF. A foreign legal entity generally applies using Form 036, supporting evidence of legal existence and authority to act, and identification documents for its representative; documents may require apostille or legalization and certified Spanish translation. A non-established taxable person making Spanish VAT-taxable supplies must register before commencing those supplies. A taxable person established outside the EU may be required to appoint a Spanish fiscal representative for VAT purposes, subject to applicable statutory exceptions and mutual-assistance arrangements. A separate EU VAT identification number is obtained through AEAT registration in the relevant census; VIES validation is available for qualifying intra-Community operators.

Default Tax Classification & Elections

Default tax classification

Entity_Level_Taxation

Available election forms

Spain has no general US-style check-the-box election for an SL. An SL is ordinarily a separate corporate income-tax taxpayer. Statutory regimes may apply when their legal conditions are met, including the regime for entities with a turnover below the applicable threshold, tax-consolidation elections for qualifying groups, and special regimes for qualifying entities or transactions. These are not entity-classification elections. Spanish hybrid-mismatch rules may deny deductions or require income inclusion in specified cases; they do not provide a general classification election.

VAT / GST & 0% Export Zero-Rating

Standard VAT / GST rate

21%

Mandatory registration threshold (Nexus)

No general domestic turnover threshold exempts an otherwise taxable person from Spanish VAT registration. A Spanish-established business generally registers through the census process before commencing taxable activity. A non-established business making taxable supplies in Spain generally must register regardless of turnover, subject to specific statutory exceptions and applicable reverse-charge rules. The EU-wide EUR 10,000 threshold applies only to specified cross-border B2C supplies and is not a general Spanish domestic registration threshold.

Export 0% zero-rating conditions

Exports of goods dispatched or transported from the VAT territory of the EU to a destination outside that territory may qualify for VAT exemption with deduction rights when the statutory conditions are met and the supplier retains reliable evidence of export. A supply of services is not automatically zero-rated because the customer or activity is offshore: the place-of-supply rules determine whether Spanish VAT applies. Services supplied to a business customer established outside Spain are generally located where that customer is established, subject to exceptions; services to non-business customers and services connected with particular activities or assets require separate analysis. Ship-crew recruitment or crew-management services must be classified and tested under the applicable place-of-supply and maritime-service rules.

  • Export customs declaration and export-release or exit-result evidence, where applicable
  • Bill of lading, air waybill, or other transport documentation identifying the goods and destination
  • Commercial invoice, sales contract, and records linking the supply to the exported goods
  • Proof of payment or other commercial records supporting the transaction; an Inward Remittance Certificate is not a general Spanish statutory export-VAT requirement
  • For services, contracts, customer business-status and establishment evidence, and records substantiating the service and its place of supply

Spain does not generally require real-time tax-authority clearance or digital stamping of every invoice. The Immediate Supply of Information (SII) requires covered taxpayers, including qualifying large businesses, VAT-group members and taxpayers registered under the monthly refund regime, to report invoice data electronically to AEAT, generally within four calendar days subject to statutory counting rules and exceptions. Spanish invoicing systems are also subject to statutory integrity, traceability and anti-alteration requirements under applicable regulations; applicable implementation dates and technical requirements should be confirmed for the relevant taxpayer and software. The separate B2B electronic-invoicing mandate is subject to implementing rules and phased application. These regimes do not constitute universal invoice pre-clearance.

Spain has no general statutory foreign-exchange repatriation deadline applicable to export proceeds. The taxpayer must substantiate the exemption or non-taxability and retain records for the applicable limitation period. Unsupported or incorrectly treated supplies may be assessed for VAT, interest and applicable penalties; deliberate or serious non-compliance can attract administrative penalties under the General Tax Law, and criminal liability may arise in cases meeting statutory thresholds and elements. Refunds improperly obtained may be recovered with interest. Penalties and recovery depend on the facts, culpability, amount and applicable procedural rules.

Stage 04

Banking & Treasury Architecture

Central-bank FX diagnosis, tier-1 local banks vs offshore digital EMI matrix, and KYC rejection defense guide.

Foreign Exchange Regime & Central Bank Policy

Current-account convertibility

Spain uses the euro and has no general exchange controls for lawful current-account or capital-account transactions. Current-account payments, including maritime staffing fees, salaries, supplier payments, interest, royalties, dividends, and service charges, are generally freely convertible and transferable through regulated payment institutions. Capital movements, including foreign direct investment, shareholder loans, capital contributions, acquisitions, and repatriation of proceeds, are also generally unrestricted, subject to sanctions, anti-money-laundering controls, beneficial-ownership identification, foreign-investment notification or screening rules where applicable, and statistical reporting. A Spanish SL may remit dividends or other lawful distributions after approval of annual accounts, satisfaction of mandatory legal-reserve requirements, and confirmation that the distribution does not impair net assets or creditor protection. Nonresident dividend withholding is generally 19%, subject to applicable tax-treaty relief and potential exemption under the EU Parent-Subsidiary regime where statutory ownership, holding-period, subject-to-tax, anti-abuse, and beneficial-owner conditions are satisfied. Interest and other payments may have different withholding outcomes. Banks normally require corporate resolutions, audited or management accounts, tax evidence, contracts, invoices, proof of source of funds, and confirmation of the economic purpose before processing large or unusual transfers.

Export proceeds surrender rules

Spain has no statutory requirement for exporters or service providers to surrender export receipts to Banco de España, no mandatory conversion ratio, and no general statutory deadline for converting foreign-currency export proceeds into euros. Export proceeds may ordinarily remain in foreign-currency accounts or be converted at the company's discretion. The company must retain commercial and customs evidence, invoices, contracts, transport records, and payment confirmations, and must comply with applicable VAT, accounting, sanctions, AML, and statistical-reporting obligations. Banco de España may require declarations concerning external assets, liabilities, cross-border transactions, or payment balances under its reporting framework; applicable thresholds, frequency, and filing method depend on the reporting category and may change. Banks may impose operational cut-off times, documentary requirements, and internal conversion controls even though no general surrender rule applies.

Central bank supervision: Banco de España, acting within the Eurosystem under the European Central Bank framework. Foreign-exchange and capital-movement rules are principally derived from the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, EU payment-services legislation, Spanish Law 19/2003 on the legal regime of capital movements and economic transactions abroad, its implementing regulations, and statistical-reporting rules administered by Banco de España. Anti-money-laundering supervision and suspicious-transaction reporting are administered through the Comisión de Prevención del Blanqueo de Capitales e Infracciones Monetarias and its Executive Service, SEPBLAC.

Offshore Digital Bank / EMI Whitelist

Cross-border EMI / Fintech rails Fit: High

Medium to High for operational collections, payments, foreign-currency balances, payroll, and card or treasury functions, provided the provider is an EU-authorised electronic-money institution or payment institution passported into Spain and supports Spanish corporate customers. An EMI account is not automatically a Spanish bank deposit account, does not necessarily provide deposit-guarantee protection, and may not support statutory capital deposit, notarised incorporation, certain government payments, cash services, documentary trade finance, or all payroll functions. Offshore digital EMIs without EU authorisation, passporting, or a regulated agent in Spain present high onboarding and continuity risk. The company should maintain a regulated Spanish bank as its primary account and use an EMI as a controlled secondary rail, with documented safeguarding, client-money segregation, account-closure, sanctions-screening, and fund-repatriation procedures.

Core KYC Rejection Triggers & Defense Dossier

Inability to identify and verify the ultimate beneficial owner, use of nominee shareholders, layered offshore ownership, bearer-like arrangements, or unexplained changes in control.

Root cause: Inability to identify and verify the ultimate beneficial owner, use of nominee shareholders, layered offshore ownership, bearer-like arrangements, or unexplained changes in control.

Defense evidence: Current articles of association, complete ownership chart through every intermediate entity to the natural-person beneficial owners, certified commercial-register extracts, passports and proof of address, beneficial-owner declarations, director resolutions, shareholder registers, and written explanations for each ownership layer. Provide certified translations or apostilles where required and ensure consistency across bank, tax, corporate, and licensing records.
Mismatch between a purported maritime crew-recruitment business and expected payment flows, including payments from vessel owners, ship managers, manning agents, seafarers, crewing intermediaries, or countries unrelated to the documented operating model.

Root cause: Mismatch between a purported maritime crew-recruitment business and expected payment flows, including payments from vessel owners, ship managers, manning agents, seafarers, crewing intermediaries, or countries unrelated to the documented operating model.

Defense evidence: Detailed business narrative, private-employment-agency or maritime-crewing authorisation, Maritime Labour Convention compliance evidence where applicable, client and vessel-owner contracts, crew-management agreements, fee schedules, sample invoices, recruitment and payroll procedures, vessel and flag-state information, staffing rosters, expected transaction matrix by country and currency, and an explanation of pass-through payroll or reimbursed-cost flows.
High-risk or sanctioned jurisdictions, politically exposed persons, vessel sanctions exposure, opaque ship ownership, payments involving sanctioned persons, or adverse media concerning maritime labor, trafficking, forced labor, or corruption.

Root cause: High-risk or sanctioned jurisdictions, politically exposed persons, vessel sanctions exposure, opaque ship ownership, payments involving sanctioned persons, or adverse media concerning maritime labor, trafficking, forced labor, or corruption.

Defense evidence: Documented sanctions and PEP screening policy, screening logs, vessel IMO numbers, flag-state and beneficial-owner checks, counterparty identification, adverse-media review, enhanced due-diligence reports, sanctions representations in contracts, escalation records, and evidence that prohibited parties and vessels are excluded. Maintain a documented approval trail for any elevated-risk relationship and obtain bank pre-clearance before processing unusual payments.
Large inbound shareholder funding, intercompany loans, capital injections, or third-party funds without a clear legal and accounting basis.

Root cause: Large inbound shareholder funding, intercompany loans, capital injections, or third-party funds without a clear legal and accounting basis.

Defense evidence: Shareholder or board resolutions, executed subscription or loan agreements, ownership and lender evidence, source-of-wealth and source-of-funds records, bank statements, audited financial statements, tax returns, capital-registration or corporate-filing evidence where applicable, purpose codes, and a reconciliation linking each incoming transfer to the accounting ledger and approved corporate purpose.
Use of personal accounts, cash-intensive settlement, rapid movement of funds through multiple payment providers, unexplained round-dollar transfers, or payments lacking invoices and contracts.

Root cause: Use of personal accounts, cash-intensive settlement, rapid movement of funds through multiple payment providers, unexplained round-dollar transfers, or payments lacking invoices and contracts.

Defense evidence: Treasury policy prohibiting personal and unapproved third-party accounts, approved bank-account list, segregation-of-duties matrix, invoice and contract archive, payment approval workflow, payroll register, reconciliation reports, cash-limit policy, transaction-monitoring alerts and resolutions, and documented explanations for any exception.

Cross-Border Clearing Corridors & Settlement Fit

Route shareholder equity, share-premium funding, and shareholder loans from an account held in the investor's own name at a regulated bank or EU payment institution into the Spanish SL's corporate account. Use a clear transfer narrative such as share capital, share premium, or shareholder loan and ensure the accounting treatment matches the legal instrument. Before transfer, provide the receiving bank with the executed subscription or loan agreement, corporate approvals, ownership chart, source-of-funds evidence, beneficial-owner information, and any required notarial, commercial-register, foreign-investment, or statistical documentation. Use SEPA Credit Transfer for euro payments where available and SWIFT or correspondent banking for non-SEPA currencies. Reconcile the transfer to the company ledger and retain MT103 or equivalent payment evidence, bank statements, foreign-exchange confirmations, and supporting contracts. Do not route capital through employees, directors, unrelated group entities, personal accounts, cash, or unlicensed offshore intermediaries. Any applicable payment-purpose classification is bank- and reporting-system-specific; use the bank's accurate capital-contribution, loan, or investment purpose rather than a generic trade or service code.Use SEPA Credit Transfer or SEPA Instant Credit Transfer for eligible euro payments within the SEPA area, subject to bank limits and beneficiary validation. Use SWIFT cross-border payment messaging, historically evidenced by MT103 and increasingly implemented through ISO 20022 payment messages, for non-SEPA or non-euro settlements. Commercial letters of credit may be issued or advised through a Spanish bank under UCP 600, with documentary examination, sanctions screening, vessel and country checks, and confirmation where commercially justified. Documentary collections may use URC 522. Pay crew wages through controlled payroll accounts or regulated payroll providers, supported by employment or placement records, wage statements, seafarer identity and assignment records, and applicable labor-law documentation. Pay suppliers and vessel operators only against verified contracts and invoices; maintain a three-way control among contract, invoice, and payment instruction. For imports or service purchases, retain customs, transport, VAT, withholding-tax, and beneficial-owner documentation where relevant. Apply dual approval, beneficiary call-back or bank verification for changes, sanctions screening, transaction limits, daily liquidity monitoring, and reconciliation of all correspondent-bank charges and foreign-exchange conversions.Deliverable forward foreign-exchange contracts with an authorised bank or investment firm, used to hedge documented forecast or committed receivables, payables, payroll, or intercompany exposures. The company should maintain hedge-purpose evidence, maturity limits, counterparty limits, valuation records, and accounting documentation.Non-deliverable forwards may be available for currencies subject to local convertibility restrictions or where physical delivery is impractical. They are bilateral derivatives, not a substitute for lawful settlement of underlying invoices, and require counterparty eligibility, ISDA or equivalent documentation, margin or collateral analysis, sanctions screening, and suitability or appropriateness procedures.Currency swaps and cross-currency interest-rate swaps may be used for longer-term funding or structural currency exposure, subject to bank approval, documented underlying exposure, collateral and close-out terms, valuation, counterparty-credit limits, and applicable EMIR risk-mitigation, reporting, clearing, and margin requirements.FX options, collars, and option combinations may be available through regulated counterparties for asymmetric exposure protection. The company must evaluate premium, leverage, knock-in or knock-out features, mark-to-market exposure, early termination risk, and board-approved risk limits.For an ordinary Spanish SL, speculative foreign-exchange trading should be prohibited by treasury policy. Derivative transactions should be executed only with regulated EU or equivalent counterparties under approved master agreements, with documented commercial exposure, authorised signatories, independent confirmation, periodic valuation, and compliance with MiFID II, EMIR, accounting, tax, and market-abuse requirements.

E-commerce / gateway settlement fit: Medium to High for operational collections, payments, foreign-currency balances, payroll, and card or treasury functions, provided the provider is an EU-authorised electronic-money institution or payment institution passported into Spain and supports Spanish corporate customers. An EMI account is not automatically a Spanish bank deposit account, does not necessarily provide deposit-guarantee protection, and may not support statutory capital deposit, notarised incorporation, certain government payments, cash services, documentary trade finance, or all payroll functions. Offshore digital EMIs without EU authorisation, passporting, or a regulated agent in Spain present high onboarding and continuity risk. The company should maintain a regulated Spanish bank as its primary account and use an EMI as a controlled secondary rail, with documented safeguarding, client-money segregation, account-closure, sanctions-screening, and fund-repatriation procedures.

Annual Statutory Maintenance

Statutory filing calendar, progressive late penalties, external audit triggers, and statutory registers.

Statutory Filing Calendar

Statutory deliverableDeadline window Government feeDelinquency sanctions
Deposit of Annual Accounts (Depósito de Cuentas Anuales): balance sheet, profit and loss account, statement of changes in equity, notes; external audit report attached when audit threshold is met. Ordinary general meeting of partners must approve accounts by 30 June (within 6 months of the 31 December year-end); deposit must be made within 1 month of approval, i.e. by 31 July for calendar-year companies. $220 USD Fine of EUR 1,200 to EUR 60,000 under Article 283 of the Ley de Sociedades de Capital; 'cierre registral' blocks registration of all further company documents until the deposit is completed; default for 3 consecutive years triggers administrative closure of the registry sheet and may lead to judicial dissolution.
Corporate Income Tax Return (Modelo 200 / Impuesto sobre Sociedades). Within 25 days following the 6-month period after the tax year-end; calendar-year SLs file by 25 July. $0 USD Late-filing surcharge under Article 27 LGT: 5% within 3 months, 10% within 6 months, 15% within 12 months, 20% beyond 12 months, plus late-payment interest of 3.75%; inaccurate or incomplete returns attract penalties of 15%-40%; failure to pay triggers enforcement embargo and may constitute criminal tax offence, but does not by itself cause registry strike-off.
Annual VAT Summary Return (Modelo 390 / Resumen Anual de IVA). Between 1 and 30 January of the year following the calendar year. $0 USD Late-filing surcharge of 5%-20% plus late-payment interest; underestimation of output VAT leads to assessment with penalties up to 20% of the omitted amount; no direct registry strike-off.
Annual Payroll Withholding Summary Return (Modelo 190 / Resumen Anual de Retenciones e Ingresos a Cuenta del IRPF) covering crew and shore staff remuneration. By 31 January of the year following the payroll year. $0 USD Late-filing surcharge of 5%-20% plus late-payment interest; incorrect or missing data items are penalised at EUR 150 per datum under Article 198 LGT; no registry strike-off.
Annual Third-Party Transaction Statement (Modelo 347) filing all counterparties (suppliers, clients, crew payroll landlords, subagents) with an annual aggregate exceeding EUR 3,000. Between 1 and 28 February of the year following the reporting year; applicable only when the EUR 3,000 threshold is exceeded. $0 USD Late-filing surcharge of 5%-20% plus late-payment interest; false or omitted data is penalised at EUR 150 per datum; no registry strike-off.
Legalization (rubrication) of statutory and accounting books via the Registro Mercantil electronic service: Register of Members, Register of Directors, Minute Book, UBO Book, Journal, Inventory and Annual Accounts Book. Within 4 months after fiscal year-end; i.e. by 30 April for calendar-year companies. $90 USD Unlegalized books are deprived of evidentiary value under Article 327 of the Código de Comercio; recurrent non-legalization may be penalised by the Registry and hinders production of statutory statements, but does not directly trigger administrative strike-off.
Annual Ultimate Beneficial Ownership Declaration (Modelo D-1 / Declaración de Titularidad Real) identifying every natural person holding directly or indirectly more than 25% or exercising control. Filed annually in conjunction with the deposit of Annual Accounts, i.e. by 31 July for calendar-year companies; re-filed within one month after any share transfer creating a new UBO and upon any control change. $0 USD Breaches of Law 10/2010: minor infringement up to EUR 60,000; serious infringement up to EUR 600,000; very serious or false declaration up to EUR 1,500,000; registry filings may be suspended until the UBO declaration is regularized.
Annual continuation filing and data refresh of the administrative authorization for seafarer recruitment and placement (Empresa de Contratación de Gente de Mar) maintained in the EGAM registry of the Spanish Maritime Administration. Annually in accordance with the granting resolution; any change in managers, registered office, financial guarantee, insurance cover or flag-state authorizations must be notified within one month. $150 USD Failure to maintain MLC 2006-compliant operating conditions or to report material changes leads to suspension or revocation of the authorization and removal from the EGAM registry; continued unlicensed activity constitutes a serious maritime-labour administrative infringement carrying monetary fines.
Annual return deadline

Ordinary general meeting of partners must approve accounts by 30 June (within 6 months of the 31 December year-end); deposit must be made within 1 month of approval, i.e. by 31 July for calendar-year companies.

Statutory government annual fee

$220 USD

Late filing penalties

Fine of EUR 1,200 to EUR 60,000 under Article 283 of the Ley de Sociedades de Capital; 'cierre registral' blocks registration of all further company documents until the deposit is completed; default for 3 consecutive years triggers administrative closure of the registry sheet and may lead to judicial dissolution.

Strike-off trigger

Mandatory Audit Threshold Mandatory Audit for All Entities

Turnover: Independent audit is compulsory for an SL when at least two of the following three thresholds are exceeded for two consecutive fiscal years: (i) total assets exceeding EUR 4,000,000; (ii) net annual turnover exceeding EUR 8,000,000; (iii) average workforce exceeding 50 employees. Audit is also mandatory for SLs preparing IFRS consolidated accounts, for entities issuing public securities, for those receiving material designated public subsidies, and for maritime-labour regulated activities when the applicable sectoral law or the Dirección General de Marina Mercante requires it.

Corporate Tax & Transfer Pricing

Corporate income tax (CIT), box-by-box return breakdown, dividend WHT, and director personal liability.

Statutory corporate income tax (CIT)

25%

Dividend withholding tax (WHT)

19% for non-resident shareholders; 0% for Spanish-resident corporate shareholders under the participation exemption / domestic withholding exemption rules.

Mandatory Return Breakdown

Deadline: · Frequency:

Within 25 calendar days after the six-month period following the fiscal year-end. For calendar-year entities, due by 25 July of the following year. For a 31 December year-end, the filing period is 1–25 July.

Box-by-Box Return Breakdown (non-resident focus)

BoxField Non-resident guidanceTax-evasion pitfall
Box 135 Identificación de la entidad (Company identification, NIF, corporate name, main activity code, and registered address). Enter the Spanish permanent establishment (PE) identification number; the PE is treated as the taxpayer for Form 200. If no PE, file Form 210 instead. Late-filing surcharges under Article 27 LGT: 5% if filed within 3 months of the deadline; 10% within 6 months; 15% within 12 months; 20% after 12 months; plus late payment interest. If the return is required by the tax authority after formal request, a fixed penalty of EUR 200 is levied; negligent omission of material data may attract penalties of 50%–150% of the resulting tax loss. Underaclaración (excessive deduction) triggers specific penalties under Article 25 LGT.

Enter the PE-specific accounting result derived from the Spanish branch's statutory accounts, not global company results. Late-filing surcharges under Article 27 LGT: 5% if filed within 3 months of the deadline; 10% within 6 months; 15% within 12 months; 20% after 12 months; plus late payment interest. If the return is required by the tax authority after formal request, a fixed penalty of EUR 200 is levied; negligent omission of material data may attract penalties of 50%–150% of the resulting tax loss. Late-filing surcharges under Article 27 LGT: 5% if filed within 3 months of the deadline; 10% within 6 months; 15% within 12 months; 20% after 12 months; plus late payment interest. Compute on the PE taxable base; note any treaty restrictions on PE attribution and deductions. Late-filing surcharges under Article 27 LGT: 5% if filed within 3 months of the deadline; 10% within 6 months; 15% within 12 months; 20% after 12 months; plus late payment interest. Claim credit for withholding taxes on remittances to the PE if treaty attributes taxing rights to Spain and such taxes are paid abroad. Late-filing surcharges under Article 27 LGT: 5% if filed within 3 months of the deadline; 10% within 6 months; 15% within 12 months; 20% after 12 months; plus late payment interest. If the return is required by the tax authority after formal request, a fixed penalty of EUR 200 is levied; negligent omission of material data may attract penalties of 50%–150% of the resulting tax loss. Verify that quarterly prepayment credits (Modelos 202/222) and Spanish-source WHTs are correctly offset; any residual tax must be paid by the deadline. If the return is required by the tax authority after formal request, a fixed penalty of EUR 200 is levied; negligent omission of material data may attract penalties of 50%–150% of the resulting tax loss. Underaclaración (excessive deduction) triggers specific penalties under Article 25 LGT.

Transfer Pricing & Economic Substance

Master / Local File threshold: Local File documentation is compulsory where related-party transaction volume exceeds EUR 250,000 in aggregate or where the taxpayer's net turnover exceeds EUR 10 million. Master File is compulsory where the group's consolidated net turnover exceeds EUR 45 million in the preceding tax year. Simplified documentation applies to entities with net turnover under EUR 10 million, provided related-party transactions remain under the EUR 250,000 aggregate threshold.

Economic substance scope: No standalone Economic Substance Regulations (ESR) exist in Spain. However, the general anti-abuse rule (GAAR) under Article 15 LGT and the substance requirements of the Spanish CIT law (e.g., tax residency, permanent establishment attribution, and DTA beneficial-ownership clauses) require a functional presence — staff, premises, and management — sufficient to perform the claimed business activities. A shell entity without local substance that book-crews or channels maritime recruitment fees through Spain faces risk of tax treaty denial, recharacterization, and anti-avoidance penalties.

Fatal Compliance Red Lines & Director Liability

Tax Evasion (Delito contra la Hacienda Pública)

Statutory sanction: Fines of 50%–150% of the defrauded tax, plus late-payment interest. Criminal conviction carries imprisonment of 1–5 years, or 2–6 years where organized fraud is proven, plus loss of subsidies and prohibition to obtain public contracts for up to 5 years.

Director personal liability: Directors who knowingly signed or consented to the false return are personally jointly and severally liable for the tax debt; in criminal cases they may be subject to arrest/surrender, passport revocation, and imprisonment (even on provisional detention).
Shell Company / Lack of Economic Substance / Treaty Abuse

Statutory sanction: AEAT disallows treaty benefits, recharacterizes the Spanish entity as a pure conduit, and applies corporate tax adjustments plus a 50% penalty on tax underpaid under Article 15 LGT (GAAR). If determined to be a sham, the entity loses limited liability at tax level and the underlying owners are taxed directly.

Director personal liability: Directors are jointly liable for recharacterized taxes and penalties if they did not maintain actual control and substance; travel restrictions and asset freezes may be imposed during criminal fraud investigations.
Transfer Pricing Non-Compliance

Statutory sanction: Transfer-pricing adjustment may be assessed with a 15% penalty on the amount of upward adjustment (in addition to interest), and a EUR 1,500–3,000 fine for documentation non-compliance or EUR 30,000–60,000 for serious documentation violations. In cases of concealment, the 50%–150% fraud penalty may apply.

Director personal liability: Directors who orchestrate artificial intercompany pricing for offshore affiliates can be held personally liable for the penalty portion if bad faith is proven; international asset tracing and travel bans may accompany criminal proceedings.
Withholding Tax & Dividend Repatriation Failure

Statutory sanction: Immediate tax debt imposed on the Spanish payer, including undeduced WHT (19% on dividends/interest, 24% on royalties), plus interest and penalties of 50%–150% for willful non-withholding; late-filing surcharges also applicable.

Director personal liability: The commercial director is jointly liable for the unpaid withholding, as the law imposes a personal responsibility on those who deliberately failed to comply with tax withholdings, including business closure or bank garnishment.
Anti-Money Laundering Violations (Ley 10/2010)

Statutory sanction: Severe infraction fines from EUR 60,001 to EUR 150,000 for failure of internal control systems; very severe violations can reach EUR 1,500,000 or 10% of net turnover. Burial in the Official State Gazette may be published.

Director personal liability: Directors who consciously fail to establish KYC/AML processes are personally liable for the fines and may face criminal money-laundering charges (articles 301–302 of the Spanish Penal Code), with imprisonment of 1–6 years in aggravated cases and prohibition to manage companies for up to 10 years.
